title: Number Bases & Binary
description: How place value works in any base — binary place values, converting between binary and base 10, why computers use binary, and a first look at hexadecimal.

notes.heading: Place Value in Base 10 (Recap)
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Base 10 (also called denary) is our everyday number system. It uses ten digits: $0, 1, 2, \ldots, 9$. The position of a digit tells you its value — each place is worth ten times the place immediately to its right.

🔑 How it works
The place values are powers of ten:
$$\ldots, \ 10^3 = 1000, \ 10^2 = 100, \ 10^1 = 10, \ 10^0 = 1$$
So a number like $4307$ really means:
$$4307 = 4 \times 1000 + 3 \times 100 + 0 \times 10 + 7 \times 1$$

💡 Worked Example
What is the value of the digit $6$ in the number $56214$?

The $6$ sits in the thousands column, so it is worth $6 \times 1000 = 6000$ — not just $6$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Moving one place to the left multiplies a digit's value by $10$.
• A $0$ is a placeholder: the $0$ in $4307$ shows there are no tens, and without it the other digits would shift.
• Every whole number can be broken into its place-value parts, and the parts add back to the original number.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Giving the face value of a digit instead of its place value. The digit $6$ in $56214$ is worth $6000$, not $6$.

✅ Check
Split the number into parts and add them: $50000 + 6000 + 200 + 10 + 4 = 56214$ — it matches.

notes.heading: What Is a Number Base?
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A number base (or radix) is the number of different digits a counting system uses — and the amount each place multiplies by as you move left.

• Base 10 (denary): ten digits, $0$–$9$; places multiply by $10$.
• Base 2 (binary): two digits, $0$ and $1$; places multiply by $2$.
• Base 16 (hexadecimal): sixteen digits; places multiply by $16$.

🔑 How it works
Any whole number can be written in any base — only the symbols change, not the value. A small subscript shows which base is meant: $1011_2$ is binary, while $25_{10}$ is ordinary base 10.

Counting shows the pattern. In base 10, when a column fills up we carry to the next column: $8, 9, 10, 11, \ldots$

Binary fills up much faster because there are only two digits:
$$0, \ 1, \ 10, \ 11, \ 100, \ 101, \ 110, \ 111, \ 1000, \ldots$$
Each of these is a perfectly good number: $10_2$ means "one two and no ones" — the value we call two.

💡 Worked Example
What comes after $111_2$ in binary?

Every column is full, so we carry all the way: the next number is $1000_2$ (which is $8$ in base 10).

📎 Key Points to Remember
• A base-$b$ system uses exactly $b$ different digits, from $0$ up to $b - 1$.
• The same value looks different in different bases: $8_{10} = 1000_2$.
• Subscripts avoid confusion when more than one base is being used.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Reading $10_2$ as "ten". In binary there is no digit $2$–$9$, so $10_2$ is the value two. Say it as "one-zero" to stay safe.

notes.heading: Binary Place Values
notes.body:
📌 Definition
In binary (base 2) the place values are powers of two instead of powers of ten. Reading from the right, each place is worth DOUBLE the one before it:
$$\ldots, \ 2^5 = 32, \ 2^4 = 16, \ 2^3 = 8, \ 2^2 = 4, \ 2^1 = 2, \ 2^0 = 1$$

🔑 How it works
• A binary number is built from digits called bits (binary digits), each $0$ or $1$.
• A $1$ in a place means "include this place value"; a $0$ means "leave it out".
• Example: $1101_2$ has place values $8, 4, 2, 1$ under its digits, so it includes $8 + 4 + 1$.

💡 Worked Example 1
What is the value of the leftmost $1$ in $10000_2$?

Count places from the right: $1, 2, 4, 8, 16$. The leftmost digit is in the fifth place, worth $2^4 = 16$.

💡 Worked Example 2
What is the largest number you can write with four bits?

Fill every place with a $1$: $1111_2 = 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15$. Notice that $15 = 2^4 - 1$ — four bits give $2^4 = 16$ different values ($0$ to $15$).

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Learn the first powers of two by heart: $1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256$.
• The rightmost place is always worth $1$ (since $2^0 = 1$).
• $n$ bits can represent $2^n$ different values, from $0$ up to $2^n - 1$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Numbering the places $1, 2, 3, 4, \ldots$ instead of $1, 2, 4, 8, \ldots$ Each binary place is double the previous one, not one more.

✅ Check
Each place value should be double the one on its right: $1, 2, 4, 8, 16$ doubles correctly every step.

notes.heading: Converting Binary to Base 10
notes.body:
📌 Definition
To convert a binary number to base 10, add up the place values of every digit that is a $1$.

🔑 How it works
1. Write the binary number down.
2. Label each digit with its place value, starting from $1$ on the RIGHT and doubling each step left.
3. Add the place values that sit above a $1$; ignore the ones above a $0$.

💡 Worked Example 1
Convert $1101_2$ to base 10.

Place values: $8, 4, 2, 1$ above the digits $1, 1, 0, 1$.
$$1101_2 = 8 + 4 + 0 + 1 = 13$$

💡 Worked Example 2
Convert $10110_2$ to base 10.

Place values: $16, 8, 4, 2, 1$ above the digits $1, 0, 1, 1, 0$.
$$10110_2 = 16 + 0 + 4 + 2 + 0 = 22$$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Always label place values starting from the RIGHT with $1$.
• Only the digits that are $1$ contribute to the total.
• More bits means bigger numbers: the leftmost place of a 6-bit number is worth $32$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Starting the place values from the left, or starting them at $2$ instead of $1$. Both scramble every conversion — always begin with $1$ at the right-hand end.

✅ Check
The answer must be odd if the binary number ends in $1$ (the units place is worth $1$) and even if it ends in $0$. $1101_2$ ends in $1$ and $13$ is odd — consistent.

notes.heading: Converting Base 10 to Binary
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Two reliable methods turn a base-10 number into binary: repeated division by $2$ (reading the remainders) and place-value subtraction (taking away the largest powers of two that fit).

🔑 How it works — repeated division
1. Divide the number by $2$ and record the remainder ($0$ or $1$).
2. Divide the answer by $2$ again, recording the new remainder.
3. Keep going until you reach $0$.
4. Read the remainders from BOTTOM to TOP — that is the binary number.

💡 Worked Example 1
Convert $13$ to binary.

$13 \div 2 = 6$ remainder $1$
$6 \div 2 = 3$ remainder $0$
$3 \div 2 = 1$ remainder $1$
$1 \div 2 = 0$ remainder $1$

Reading upwards: $13 = 1101_2$.

🔑 How it works — place-value subtraction
1. Find the largest power of two that is not bigger than the number; write a $1$ and subtract it.
2. Move to the next power down: if it fits into what is left, write $1$ and subtract; if not, write $0$.
3. Continue down to $1$.

💡 Worked Example 2
Convert $45$ to binary.

$45 - 32 = 13$ → $1$ in the $32$s place
$16$ does not fit into $13$ → $0$
$13 - 8 = 5$ → $1$ in the $8$s place
$5 - 4 = 1$ → $1$ in the $4$s place
$2$ does not fit into $1$ → $0$
$1 - 1 = 0$ → $1$ in the $1$s place

So $45 = 101101_2$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Repeated division: remainders read UPWARD.
• Subtraction method: work from the LARGEST power of two downward.
• Both methods must give the same answer.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Reading the remainders top-to-bottom. That gives the digits in reverse — $13$ would wrongly come out as $1011_2$ (which is $11$).

✅ Check
Convert your answer back: $101101_2 = 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 45$ — it matches.

notes.heading: Why Computers Use Binary
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Computers store and process everything — numbers, text, images, sound, video — using binary, because their circuits are built from millions of tiny switches that each have exactly two states: ON or OFF.

🔑 How it works
• A switch that is ON can represent $1$; OFF represents $0$.
• Each single binary digit is called a bit. A group of $8$ bits is a byte.
• Two states are far more reliable than ten: a circuit only has to tell "high voltage" from "low voltage", so small electrical fluctuations do not corrupt the data.
• Logic circuits combine bits using simple rules, and every operation a computer performs — from addition to displaying this page — is built from those rules.

💡 Worked Example
How many different values can one byte ($8$ bits) represent?
$$2^8 = 256 \text{ values, from } 0 \text{ to } 255$$
That is why many systems — like the red, green and blue levels in a digital colour — use numbers from $0$ to $255$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Binary matches the two-state nature of electronic switches.
• Reliability, not speed for humans, is the reason computers use base 2.
• A bit is one binary digit; a byte is eight bits.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Thinking computers "prefer" binary because it is simpler maths. The maths is the same — the choice is driven by hardware: two states are easy and dependable to build and detect.

✅ Check
Any device that stores data in two distinct states (magnetised/not magnetised, pit/no pit on a disc) is using binary thinking.

notes.heading: Hexadecimal — A First Look
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Hexadecimal is base 16. It needs sixteen digits, so after $0$–$9$ it borrows letters:
$$0, 1, 2, \ldots, 9, \ A, B, C, D, E, F$$
where $A = 10$, $B = 11$, $C = 12$, $D = 13$, $E = 14$ and $F = 15$.

🔑 How it works
• Hexadecimal is popular in computing because ONE hex digit matches exactly FOUR bits: $2^4 = 16$.
• So $F_{16} = 15 = 1111_2$, and $A_{16} = 10 = 1010_2$.
• Long binary strings become short and readable: $10101100_2$ splits into $1010$ and $1100$, which are $A$ and $C$ — so the value is $AC_{16}$.

💡 Worked Example
Write the binary number $00101100_2$ in hexadecimal.

Split into two groups of four bits: $0010$ and $1100$.
$0010_2 = 2$ and $1100_2 = 12 = C$.
So $00101100_2 = 2C_{16}$.

Where you will meet it: memory addresses, error codes, and colour codes on the web (for example, pure red is written #FF0000 — the FF is a byte written in hex).

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Base 16 uses digits $0$–$9$ plus letters $A$–$F$.
• Each hex digit stands for exactly four binary digits.
• Hex is a human-friendly shorthand for binary — computers still work in bits.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Treating $A$–$F$ as letters with no value. In hexadecimal they are digits: $F$ is worth $15$, so $10_{16}$ is sixteen, not ten.

✅ Check
Convert each hex digit to four bits and back: $C = 12 = 1100_2$ and $1100_2 = 8 + 4 = 12$ — consistent.

flashcards.definition: The number of different digits a counting system uses, and the amount each place value multiplies by.
flashcards.example: Base 10 uses ten digits $0$–$9$; base 2 uses two digits, $0$ and $1$.

flashcards.definition: The everyday number system with digits $0$–$9$, where each place is worth ten times the place to its right.
A number system using only the digits $0$ and $1$, where each place value is a power of two.
A single binary digit — a $0$ or a $1$. Short for "binary digit".
A group of $8$ bits, able to represent $2^8 = 256$ different values.
flashcards.example: One byte can hold any whole number from $0$ to $255$.

flashcards.definition: From the right: $1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, \ldots$ — each place is double the one before it.
flashcards.example: In $10110_2$ the leftmost digit sits in the $16$s place.

flashcards.definition: Label each digit with its place value starting at $1$ on the right, then add the values above every $1$.
Divide by $2$ repeatedly, record each remainder, then read the remainders from bottom to top.
Repeatedly subtract the largest power of two that fits, writing $1$ where it fits and $0$ where it does not.
A base-16 system using digits $0$–$9$ and letters $A$–$F$ for the values $10$ to $15$.

flashcards.term: Number of values from n bits
flashcards.definition: $n$ bits can represent $2^n$ different values, from $0$ up to $2^n - 1$.
Electronic circuits have two reliable states (on/off), matching the two binary digits and making data hard to corrupt.
flashcards.example: A switch ON represents $1$ and OFF represents $0$; eight switches store one byte.

questions.stem: How many different digits does the binary system use?
questions.explanation: Binary is base 2, so it uses exactly two digits: $0$ and $1$. Base 10 is the system with ten digits.

choices: A group of eight binary digits
The base-10 value of a binary number
The leftmost digit of any number
questions.explanation: A bit is one binary digit (short for binary digit). Eight bits together make a byte, which is the first option.
The place values are $16, 8, 4, 2, 1$; the $1$s sit above $16$, $8$ and $2$, giving $16 + 8 + 2 = 26$.
$50 = 32 + 16 + 2$, giving $110010_2$. The distractors convert to $42$, $58$ and $52$ — check by adding the place values back.

questions.stem: In binary, the place values run $1, 2, 4, 8, 16, \ldots$ from the right. What is the next place value after $16$?
questions.explanation: Each binary place is double the one before it, so the place after $16$ is $2 \times 16 = 32$.

questions.stem: What is the largest number that can be written using exactly four bits?
questions.explanation: Four bits all set to $1$ give $1111_2 = 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15$, which is $2^4 - 1$. Four bits give $16$ values in total, but counting starts at $0$.

questions.stem: Why do computers use binary rather than base 10?
choices: Binary numbers are shorter to write down
Electronic circuits have two reliable states, on and off, which match the two binary digits
questions.explanation: Circuits only need to distinguish two states (high or low voltage), which map directly onto $1$ and $0$ and resist electrical noise. Binary numbers are actually longer than base-10 ones.

questions.stem: In hexadecimal, what value does the digit $A$ represent?
questions.explanation: Hexadecimal continues past $9$ with letters: $A = 10$, $B = 11$, up to $F = 15$.
Six bits mean place values $32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1$. The $1$s are above $32$, $8$, $4$ and $1$: $32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 45$.
$77 = 64 + 8 + 4 + 1$, so the $64$, $8$, $4$ and $1$ places get a $1$: $1001101_2$. The other options convert to $75$, $89$ and $78$.

questions.stem: Which statement is always true about an odd number written in binary?
choices: It has an even number of digits
questions.explanation: Every binary place value except the units place is even, so a number is odd exactly when its units digit is $1$. For example, $13 = 1101_2$ ends in $1$.

questions.stem: The hexadecimal digit $B$ is written as which four-bit binary value?
questions.explanation: $B = 11$, and one hex digit equals four bits: $11 = 8 + 2 + 1 = 1011_2$. Option A is $10$ (hex $A$) and $1100_2$ is $12$ (hex $C$).
The single $1$ is in the seventh place from the right, worth $2^6 = 64$. Each extra zero on the right doubles the value: $1, 10_2 = 2, 100_2 = 4, \ldots, 1000000_2 = 64$.
